name: Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures (29 CFR 1607)
what: The 1978 framework the EEOC, DOL, DOJ and the Civil Service Commission adopted for judging selection procedures under Title VII [30](#cite:30). It expects records of selection rates by sex and by race or ethnic group, treats a group selection rate below [four-fifths](#term:four-fifths-rule) of the highest group's as generally evidencing [adverse impact](#term:adverse-impact), and generally does not expect component validation when the overall process shows no impact [31](#cite:31). A procedure with adverse impact needs criterion-related, content or construct validity evidence tied to important elements of job performance, cutoffs set to normal expectations of proficiency, and more evidence for ranking than for pass/fail use [32](#cite:32).
applies_when: Any employer covered by Title VII using any selection procedure, including algorithmic tools used to make or inform decisions [35](#cite:35)
steps: Keep selection-rate records by sex and by race or ethnic group (sampling allowed at high volume) [31](#cite:31)
Compare each group's rate to the highest group's; investigate below four-fifths, with statistical and practical significance in mind [31](#cite:31)
Hold validity evidence (criterion, content or construct) for any procedure with adverse impact; more for ranking than pass/fail [32](#cite:32)
Document per 1607.15 (not read this sweep; todo)

name: Title VII, ADA and ADEA rules on tests and selection procedures (EEOC fact sheet)
what: The EEOC's technical assistance of December 1, 2007 maps the three statutes onto selection: disparate treatment is intentional; [disparate impact](#term:disparate-impact) is a neutral procedure that disproportionately excludes a protected group and must be job-related and consistent with business necessity, with a less discriminatory alternative available to the challenger; the ADA bars [disability-related questions](#term:pre-employment-inquiry) and medical exams before a conditional offer; the ADEA permits neutral practices affecting workers 40 and older only on a reasonable factor other than age [33](#cite:33). Vendor documentation helps but the employer stays responsible for validation [33](#cite:33).
governing_text: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964; Americans with Disabilities Act; Age Discrimination in Employment Act
applies_when: All covered employers using cognitive or physical tests, work samples and simulations, medical inquiries, personality or integrity tests, background or credit checks, appraisals or English-proficiency tests [33](#cite:33)
steps: Administer tests without regard to protected characteristics [33](#cite:33)
Validate for the specific job and purpose; obtain vendor documentation but own the responsibility [33](#cite:33)
If a procedure screens out a protected group, look for an equally effective alternative with less impact and adopt it if one exists [33](#cite:33)
Update test specifications as the job changes [33](#cite:33)

name: ADA limits on pre-offer disability questions and medical examinations
what: Before a conditional offer an employer may not ask [disability-related questions](#term:pre-employment-inquiry), defined as questions likely to elicit information about a disability, or require medical examinations; it may ask whether the applicant can perform job functions with or without reasonable accommodation, may ask for a demonstration if everyone in the category is asked, and may ask about licences, attendance and arrest or conviction records [34](#cite:34). After a conditional offer, medical questions and exams are allowed if required of everyone entering the job category; a withdrawn offer must be job-related and consistent with business necessity, or rest on a direct threat for safety exclusions [34](#cite:34). Physical agility and fitness tests are not medical unless physiological responses are measured; psychological tests are medical if they can identify a mental disorder; tests for current illegal drug use are not medical examinations [34](#cite:34).
governing_text: Americans with Disabilities Act, 42 U.S.C. 12112(d); EEOC Enforcement Guidance 915.002 (October 10, 1995)
applies_when: Every covered employer at the application, interview and conditional-offer steps; the 1995 guidance predates the ADA Amendments Act of 2008 [34](#cite:34)
steps: Pre-offer: ask about ability to perform job functions with or without accommodation; ask whether accommodation is needed for the hiring process [34](#cite:34)
Post-offer: medical inquiries and exams only if applied to all entering employees in the same job category [34](#cite:34)
Keep the offer "real": evaluate all reasonably obtainable non-medical information before extending it [34](#cite:34)

name: Criminal records under Title VII (EEOC 2012 guidance)
what: A criminal-record policy that disproportionately screens out a protected group must be job-related and consistent with business necessity; the EEOC accepts a validated screen or a targeted screen built on the nature and gravity of the offence, the time elapsed and the nature of the job, paired with an individualised assessment in which the person can respond [47](#cite:47). Exclusions based on an arrest alone are generally not job-related; a conviction is usually sufficient evidence of conduct [47](#cite:47). Federal statutes and regulations that bar people with certain records from certain jobs are a defence, but only as far as the federal requirement reaches; for [cleared](#term:security-clearance) work the [national security exception](#term:national-security-exception) applies only where the position is actually subject to federal security requirements and the action followed a clearance denial [47](#cite:47).
governing_text: Title VII; EEOC Enforcement Guidance 915.002 (April 25, 2012); Green v. Missouri Pacific Railroad (8th Cir. 1977)
applies_when: Any employer using criminal history in selection; federal contractors additionally under the Fair Chance Act (fair-chance-act-contractors)
steps: Eliminate blanket exclusions; write a targeted screen naming disqualifying offences and justified durations [47](#cite:47)
Give an individualised assessment: notify, allow a response, weigh circumstances, age at conviction, work history, rehabilitation [47](#cite:47)
Limit inquiries to records that would actually justify exclusion; keep the information confidential [47](#cite:47)

name: Federal Fair Chance Act (criminal-history timing for federal contractors)
what: Since December 20, 2021, federal contractors may not ask about or seek an applicant's criminal history for positions within the scope of a federal contract until after a conditional offer, under the [Fair Chance Act](#term:fair-chance-act) enacted in the FY2020 National Defense Authorization Act of December 20, 2019 [48](#cite:48). Exceptions cover positions with law-enforcement or national-security duties, positions requiring access to classified information, and positions where a law requires the inquiry earlier; a first violation brings a notice and warning and later violations can suspend payments under the contract [48](#cite:48).
governing_text: Fair Chance to Compete for Jobs Act of 2019 (Pub. L. 116-92, FY2020 NDAA); implementing FAR clause TODO(author)
applies_when: Federal contractors hiring for positions related to work under a federal contract; largely exempts cleared positions [48](#cite:48)
steps: Remove criminal-history questions from applications and interviews for contract positions; ask after the conditional offer [48](#cite:48)
Confirm whether the position falls in an exception (classified access, national security, law enforcement, statutory requirement) [48](#cite:48)
conflicts: Only a law-firm summary was read; the FAR subpart and clause number and the OPM exclusion regulations must be confirmed from primary text (todo t-P008).

name: Citizenship-status discrimination in export-controlled hiring (8 U.S.C. 1324b)
what: An employer may not limit a job to U.S. citizens, or to citizens and permanent residents, unless a law, regulation, executive order or government contract requires it; [ITAR](#term:itar) and [EAR](#term:ear) do not, because the export rules' "[U.S. person](#term:us-person)" matches the protected-individual definition in 8 U.S.C. 1324b(a)(3): citizens, nationals, lawful permanent residents, refugees and asylees [49](#cite:49). There is no good-faith exception [49](#cite:49). DOJ's Civil Rights Division fact sheet of April 18, 2023 says not to state that export rules require a citizenship, to make clear U.S. persons includes more than citizens, to keep export assessments separate from [Form I-9](#term:form-i-9), and not to limit which I-9 documents a worker presents [51](#cite:51). Settlements include Georgia Tech (\$500,000, August 2023), more than \$2.5 million across job-platform users (2022–2023), General Motors (\$365,000, April 2023) and American CyberSystems (May 2023) [49](#cite:49) [50](#cite:50).
governing_text: 8 U.S.C. 1324b; 22 CFR 120 (ITAR) and 15 CFR 772 (EAR) definitions of U.S. person; DOJ IER employer fact sheet (April 18, 2023)
applies_when: Any posting or screen for work involving ITAR- or EAR-controlled items or technical data [131](#cite:131) [49](#cite:49); any employer with four or more employees under 1324b (threshold not read this sweep; todo)
steps: Write postings that admit all U.S. persons; never "U.S. citizens only" for export reasons [51](#cite:51) [50](#cite:50)
Run export-compliance screening as a separate step from Form I-9, and let workers choose their I-9 documents [51](#cite:51) [49](#cite:49)
Restrict by citizenship only where a law or a government contract requires it, and cite that requirement [49](#cite:49)

name: Automated and AI screening tools (federal framework and state laws)
what: Federally, an [algorithmic tool](#term:algorithmic-screening) used to make or inform a selection decision is a selection procedure under the [Uniform Guidelines](#term:uniform-guidelines) and the employer answers for a vendor's tool, as the EEOC stated on May 18, 2023 in technical assistance it removed on January 27, 2025; the Title VII rules it restated remain in force [35](#cite:35) [36](#cite:36). New York City Local Law 144 requires a bias audit no more than a year old, a published summary and candidate notice, with penalties of \$500–\$1,500 a day [37](#cite:37). Illinois Public Act 103-0804 bars discriminatory use of AI in employment decisions and requires notice from January 1, 2026; the Department of Human Rights withdrew its proposed clarifying rules on June 2, 2026 [38](#cite:38). California's Civil Rights Council regulations, effective October 1, 2025, define [automated-decision systems](#term:automated-employment-decision-tool), extend liability to agents, treat anti-bias testing before and after adoption as a defence factor, and require four-year retention of ADS records [40](#cite:40). Colorado's SB 24-205 was delayed to June 30, 2026 by SB25B-004 with amendments expected [39](#cite:39).
governing_text: Title VII and 29 CFR 1607 (federal); NYC Local Law 144 of 2021; Illinois Public Act 103-0804; 2 CCR 11008 et seq. (California); Colorado SB 24-205 as amended by SB25B-004
applies_when: Any employer using software, algorithms or AI to screen, rank, score or interview candidates; state duties attach by the candidate's or the job's location [37](#cite:37) [38](#cite:38) [40](#cite:40)
steps: Ask the vendor whether the tool was tested for substantially lower selection rates by group and by what standard [35](#cite:35)
New York City: obtain the bias audit, publish the summary, notify candidates [37](#cite:37)
Illinois: give notice when AI is used to influence or facilitate a covered decision [38](#cite:38)
California: test for bias before and after adoption and keep ADS records four years [40](#cite:40)
Colorado: confirm the law's status after June 30, 2026 before relying on it (todo)

pending_changes.text: EEOC removed its May 2023 AI technical assistance from its website; the underlying law did not change [36](#cite:36) [35](#cite:35).
Illinois IDHR withdrew and postponed its proposed notice rules; the statute remains in effect [38](#cite:38).
Colorado SB25B-004 moved the AI Act's effective date to 2026-06-30; substantive amendments were expected in the 2026 session and must be checked [39](#cite:39).

Colorado SB 26-189 (signed 2026-05-14) repealed and reenacted the Act: notice before ADMT materially influences an employment decision, an explanation within 30 days of an adverse outcome, human review and three-year records from 2027-01-01; SB 24-205 never took effect after the stipulated non-enforcement order of 2026-04-27 [222](#cite:222) [221](#cite:221).

Connecticut SB 5 (employer notice from 2027-10-01), Delaware HB 380 (2027-01-01) and three California bills (AB 1883, SB 951 from 2027-01-01; SB 947 from 2027-07-01) add duties listed in the October 2026 chart; states.yaml carries them with the statutes pending [220](#cite:220).

conflicts: The Illinois and California entries rest on secondary alerts; Colorado now has the legislature's fiscal note [222](#cite:222); the per-state overlay is states.yaml (sweep 8) with the statutes pending (t-8001).

name: VEVRAA mandatory job listing (41 CFR 60-300.5(a)(2))
what: A covered federal contractor lists every employment opening, at every establishment and whether or not the opening is contract-funded, with the appropriate employment service delivery system where the opening occurs, at least concurrently with any other recruiting; listing with the state workforce agency job bank satisfies it [73](#cite:73). Executive and senior management positions, positions filled from within, and positions of three days or less are excepted [73](#cite:73). The contractor tells the ESDS in each state that it is a federal contractor, that it wants priority [referral](#term:referral-hiring) of [protected veterans](#term:vevraa), and gives its hiring locations and contacts; the listing must accept referrals of veterans and nonveterans alike [73](#cite:73).
governing_text: Vietnam Era Veterans' Readjustment Assistance Act, 38 U.S.C. 4212; 41 CFR 60-300.5(a)(2)
applies_when: Contracts at or above the VEVRAA threshold (\$200,000 under the 2026 update [55](#cite:55); the printed clause still shows a \$100,000 subcontract flow-down figure [73](#cite:73)); the written AAP applies at 50 employees and a covered contract [55](#cite:55)
steps: Post every opening to the state workforce agency job bank no later than other recruiting [73](#cite:73)
Notify the ESDS of contractor status, hiring sites, contacts and any outside search firms; update on change [73](#cite:73)
Keep the veteran applicant and hire data that remains required after the 2026 rule [55](#cite:55)

pending_changes.text: VEVRAA regulations updated; coverage threshold \$200,000; written AAP and veteran applicant and hire reporting remain [55](#cite:55).

conflicts: Threshold: the clause text read shows \$100,000 for subcontract flow-down [73](#cite:73); the 2026 final rule reports \$200,000 [55](#cite:55). The amended 60-300.5 text is a todo.

name: Age-preference terms in help-wanted ads (29 CFR 1625.4)
what: An ad that uses terms such as "age 25 to 35", "young", "college student", "recent college graduate", "boy" or "girl" indicates an unlawful preference against workers forty and older unless a statutory exception applies; preferences for older workers ("over age 60", "retirees") are permitted; asking an applicant's age is scrutinised for a lawful purpose [78](#cite:78).
governing_text: Age Discrimination in Employment Act; 29 CFR 1625.4
applies_when: Any employer covered by the ADEA writing a job advertisement or application [78](#cite:78)
steps: Remove the listed age terms from postings and campus-recruiting copy [78](#cite:78)

name: Pay ranges in job postings (state and local laws)
what: Thirteen states and the District of Columbia require a pay range in the posting itself, at thresholds from one employee (Colorado, DC) to fifty (Hawaii): California (15+), Colorado (1+), Delaware (26+, from September 26, 2027), Hawaii (50+), Illinois (15+), Maryland, Massachusetts (25+), Minnesota (30+), New Jersey (10+), New York (4+), Vermont (5+), Washington (15+) and DC (1+), with local rules in Ohio cities and parts of New Jersey and New York; Connecticut, Rhode Island and Nevada require ranges at other points, not in the posting [76](#cite:76). By May 2025, 59 percent of US postings carried a salary figure regardless [75](#cite:75). Within a title, a 10 percent higher posted wage draws 7.7 percent more applicants [65](#cite:65).
governing_text: state statutes (sweep-8 primaries); California SB 642 effective 2026-01-01 clarifies "pay scale" [76](#cite:76)
applies_when: Postings for work performed in, or open to applicants in, a covered jurisdiction [76](#cite:76) [207](#cite:207); remote postings reachable from a covered state are commonly treated as covered [76](#cite:76) (secondary; the statutes are a todo)
steps: Show a good-faith range in every posting; the rule attaches by jurisdiction and the range is also the strongest applicant-count [lever](#term:lever-record) [65](#cite:65) [76](#cite:76)

pending_changes.text: Virginia requires a wage or salary range in every public and internal posting and bans [salary-history inquiries](#term:salary-history-ban), with a private right of action after a 15-day cure notice [223](#cite:223) [224](#cite:224).
Maine requires a pay range in every posting for employers with ten or more employees [223](#cite:223) [224](#cite:224).
Connecticut PA 26-12 requires the wage or wage range and a benefits description in every advertisement, for all employers [224](#cite:224).
Delaware's posting requirement (more than 25 employees) takes effect [76](#cite:76) [223](#cite:223).

conflicts: The jurisdiction list rests on law-firm summaries [76](#cite:76) [207](#cite:207) [223](#cite:223) [224](#cite:224); states.yaml carries the per-state overlay (sweep 8) with the statutes pending (t-8001); the DOL Women's Bureau map [208](#cite:208) exists but its table is an image.

name: The contractor EEO framework after the EO 11246 rescission (41 CFR 60-1 ff. removed)
what: From October 26, 2026 the regulations issued under [Executive Order 11246](#term:executive-order-11246) are removed: 41 CFR parts 60-1, 60-2, 60-3, 60-4, 60-20, 60-40, 60-50 and 60-999, with the EO 11246 content stripped from part 60-30 [86](#cite:86). With part 60-1 go the Internet Applicant definition and the online-recruiting [recordkeeping](#term:applicant-record-retention) rule of 2006 [87](#cite:87) [86](#cite:86). What remains for contractors is statutory: [Section 503](#term:section-503) (written [AAP](#term:vevraa) at 50 employees and a \$50,000 contract; threshold \$20,000; the 7 percent goal and applicant self-identification rescinded) and VEVRAA (written AAP; threshold \$200,000; veteran applicant and hire reporting kept), both effective September 21, 2026 [55](#cite:55). Executive Order 14173, signed January 21, 2025, revoked the order at Sec. 3(b)(i) and allowed ninety days of continued compliance with the scheme in effect on January 20, 2025, a wind-down [OFCCP](#term:ofccp) dates to April 21, 2025 [308](#cite:308) [310](#cite:310). Title VII and the [Uniform Guidelines](#term:uniform-guidelines) are unchanged [30](#cite:30) [31](#cite:31).
governing_text: 91 FR 54444 (August 21, 2026); EO 14173 (January 2025); 41 CFR 60-300 and 60-741 as amended
applies_when: Every federal contractor and subcontractor from 2026-10-26 [86](#cite:86); the EEO-1 filing duty and the Internet Applicant rule's fate are to be confirmed from the unread portion of the rule [86](#cite:86) [87](#cite:87) (todo)
steps: Stop maintaining EO 11246 AAPs after 2026-10-26; keep the Section 503 and VEVRAA plans and the veteran applicant data [55](#cite:55) [86](#cite:86)
Keep Uniform Guidelines selection-rate records regardless [31](#cite:31)

pending_changes.text: EO 11246 implementing regulations rescinded [86](#cite:86).
Section 503 and VEVRAA regulations updated [55](#cite:55).

conflicts: Whether the EEO-1 filing duty (60-1.7) survives in another instrument and whether the Internet Applicant definition is removed in terms were not in the portion of the rule read; the Section 503/VEVRAA details rest on a law-firm alert [55](#cite:55).

name: Labor-category rates and qualifications under T&M and labor-hour contracts (FAR 16.601; 52.232-7)
what: A [time-and-materials](#term:time-and-materials-contract) or labor-hour contract pays fixed hourly rates per [labor category](#term:labor-category) that include wages, [overhead](#term:overhead-rate), [G&A](#term:general-and-administrative-rate) and profit, for labor that meets the category's qualifications [98](#cite:98). Hours performed by employees who do not meet the qualifications are not paid unless the contracting officer authorises it, and vouchers must be supported by records showing qualifications [99](#cite:99). Where not competitively awarded, separate rates apply to the contractor, each [subcontractor](#term:subcontractor) and each affiliate [98](#cite:98).
applies_when: Any T&M or labor-hour contract or order; the labor-category qualifications in the contract decide who can be billed [99](#cite:99)
steps: Read the [labor-category qualifications](#term:labor-category-qualifications) before writing the posting; a candidate who does not meet them cannot be billed [99](#cite:99)
Derive the affordable salary from the rate less indirect costs and [fee](#term:fee) ([synthesis](#term:synthesis-marker) from [98](#cite:98))
Seek CO authorisation before billing anyone who does not meet the category [99](#cite:99)

name: Compensation allowability on cost-type contracts (FAR 31.205-6)
what: Compensation is [allowable](#term:allowable-cost) when reasonable for the work and conforming to an established plan or consistent practice; reasonableness is judged against firms of similar size, industry and area doing similar non-government work; no presumption of allowability attaches to major plan changes made without the administrative contracting officer's chance to review; bonuses are allowable only under a pre-existing agreement or plan; severance and pension supplements are limited; compensation above the [OFPP benchmark](#term:compensation-cap) is unallowable for all employees on awards from June 24, 2014 [100](#cite:100). The benchmark was \$671,000 for 2025 by an accounting firm's figure [107](#cite:107).
applies_when: Cost-reimbursement contracts and any contract where allowability is determined under FAR Part 31 [100](#cite:100)
steps: Keep a written compensation plan; apply it consistently [100](#cite:100)
Adopt any bonus plan before the services it rewards [100](#cite:100)
Give the ACO a chance to review major plan changes [100](#cite:100)
conflicts: The benchmark amount rests on an accounting firm's page [107](#cite:107); the OFPP determination is a todo.

name: Service Contract Act wage determinations and the health-and-welfare rate
what: Federal service contracts over \$2,500 whose principal purpose is services by service employees must pay the locally prevailing wages and fringe benefits in the [wage determination](#term:wage-determination) attached to the contract, generally drawn from BLS [OEWS](#term:oews) data, plus vacation and holiday pay [101](#cite:101). The [health-and-welfare rate](#term:health-and-welfare-rate) is \$5.55 per hour from July 2025 (\$5.09 where EO 13706 also applies; Hawaii \$2.42/\$1.96) [101](#cite:101). EO 14026's higher contractor minimum was revoked by EO 14236 on March 14, 2025 and is no longer enforced; EO 13658 remains for contracts entered or renewed January 1, 2015–January 29, 2022, at \$13.65 from May 11, 2026 [102](#cite:102) [101](#cite:101).
governing_text: 41 U.S.C. chapter 67; 29 CFR part 4; FAR subpart 22.10; EO 13658; EO 14236
applies_when: Service contracts over \$2,500 with service employees; wage determinations by locality on SAM.gov; conformance for unlisted classifications [101](#cite:101)
steps: Read the wage determination attached to the contract; the listed rate and the H&W amount are floors [101](#cite:101)
Check whether the contract falls in the EO 13658 window [102](#cite:102)

pending_changes.text: EO 14236 §2(d) revoked EO 14026; DOL will rescind 29 CFR part 23 [102](#cite:102).
EO 13658 rate \$13.65 (non-tipped) and \$9.55 (tipped) [102](#cite:102).

name: Price and labor-rate adjustment limits on schedule and T&M contracts
what: A labor rate fixed at award moves only through the contract's adjustment clause. On GSA Multiple Award Schedule contracts the economic price adjustment clause allows at most three increases per contract period, requested from thirty days after the period starts to sixty days before it ends, thirty days apart, with contracting-officer approval for increases other than ten percent; GSA suspended those limits from March 17 to September 30, 2022 when inflation outran them [117](#cite:117). The [ECI](#term:employment-cost-index) wage series the government itself uses rose 3.1 percent in the year to June 2026 [103](#cite:103).
governing_text: GSAR 552.216-70 (and I-FSS-969, 552.216-71); FAR 16.203 for economic price adjustment generally
applies_when: GSA schedule contracts and, by their own clauses, other T&M and labor-hour vehicles
steps: Diary the request window; prepare the evidence (ECI, CALC+ comparables) before it opens [117](#cite:117) [103](#cite:103) [111](#cite:111)
conflicts: The clause terms rest on a 2022 law-firm note [117](#cite:117); the current GSAR text and GSA's 2025 pricing-policy changes are a sweep-7 todo.

name: Equal Pay Act and pay discrimination (EPA; Title VII)
what: Men and women must receive equal pay for [substantially equal work](#term:equal-pay-act) (skill, effort, responsibility, working conditions) in the same establishment; differences are lawful only on seniority, merit, quantity or quality of production, or a factor other than sex, with the employer carrying the burden; no one's pay may be cut to close a gap [112](#cite:112). In the Ninth Circuit prior salary, alone or in combination, is not a factor other than sex; the Seventh Circuit holds otherwise [116](#cite:116). Title VII, the ADEA and the ADA also prohibit pay discrimination without the same-establishment or substantially-equal requirements [112](#cite:112).
governing_text: 29 U.S.C. 206(d); Title VII; Rizo v. Yovino (9th Cir. en banc 2020)
applies_when: Every covered employer setting pay; state equal-pay laws may be broader (sweep 8)
steps: Justify any differential with a documented job-related factor [112](#cite:112)
Cure gaps upward [112](#cite:112)
Do not rely on prior pay to justify a difference [116](#cite:116)
conflicts: Circuit split on prior pay [116](#cite:116); state laws vary (states.yaml, sweep 8).

name: Salary-history bans (state and local)
what: About twenty states bar all employers from asking applicants about salary history, with public-employer-only bans elsewhere and local ordinances on top; several states permit asking or confirming only after an offer, and Michigan and Wisconsin have ended bans for most employers [106](#cite:106). The early bans raised women's earnings relative to men's by about 1 percent, mainly among job changers [96](#cite:96).
governing_text: state statutes (sweep-8 primaries)
applies_when: Applicants in a covered state or locality; the rule attaches to the question, however asked [106](#cite:106)
steps: Remove prior- and current-pay questions from applications, screens and interviews [106](#cite:106)
Where confirmation after an offer is permitted, document that it followed the offer [106](#cite:106)

pending_changes.text: Virginia bars [salary-history inquiries](#term:salary-history-ban) and reliance for all employers under its 2026 [pay-transparency law](#term:pay-range-posting-law) [223](#cite:223).

conflicts: The jurisdiction list rests on a vendor page [106](#cite:106) and the Mercer roundup [207](#cite:207), which disagree on Missouri; states.yaml carries the per-state overlay (sweep 8) with the statutes pending (t-8001).

name: Key-personnel availability in proposals (GAO and the Court of Federal Claims)
what: At GAO an offeror with actual knowledge that a proposed key person has become unavailable before award must notify the agency; the agency then rejects the proposal as unacceptable or reopens discussions, and the duty applies to protesters as well as awardees [108](#cite:108). The Court of Federal Claims declined to impose that duty absent a solicitation provision, requiring only a reasonable belief at submission [109](#cite:109). Declarations of continued availability have defeated dismissal motions [114](#cite:114).
governing_text: GAO bid-protest decisions (Orion Government Services, B-422978, 2024); Golden IT v. United States (COFC 2022); the solicitation's key-personnel clause
applies_when: Any competition in which the proposal names key personnel; the solicitation's own notice terms control [109](#cite:109)
steps: Read the solicitation's key-personnel and notice terms [109](#cite:109)
Keep letters of commitment current; notify promptly on unavailability [108](#cite:108) [114](#cite:114)
conflicts: GAO and the COFC differ on the duty to notify [108](#cite:108) [109](#cite:109).

name: Personnel clearance eligibility and sponsorship under the NISPOM rule (32 CFR 117.10)
what: A contractor may request eligibility only where access is essential to a classified contract, for the minimum number of employees, never to build a cache of [cleared](#term:security-clearance) staff, and never for non-employees or [subcontractor employees](#term:subcontractor) [119](#cite:119). A request before employment needs a written commitment the candidate accepted in writing, and employment must begin within 45 days of the grant [119](#cite:119). [Temporary eligibility](#term:temporary-eligibility) is available only where no adverse information appears, for up to a year, valid at its level but not for RD, COMSEC or NATO information until the final grant; its withdrawal is not a denial and cannot be appealed [119](#cite:119). An eligibility held elsewhere is accepted under SEAD 7 and access may be restored after a break in employment without a new investigation where eligibility continued [119](#cite:119). On notice of a denial, suspension or revocation the contractor removes the employee from access at once [119](#cite:119). A non-U.S. citizen can hold only a [Limited Access Authorization](#term:limited-access-authorization), in rare cases, never for [Top Secret](#term:top-secret), RD, COMSEC, intelligence or NATO information [119](#cite:119).
governing_text: 32 CFR part 117 (NISPOM rule, 85 FR 83300), §117.10
applies_when: Any contractor in the National Industrial Security Program requesting or holding personnel clearance eligibility for an employee [119](#cite:119)
steps: Confirm the classified contract and the access the position needs [119](#cite:119)
Obtain the written commitment before a pre-employment request; plan a start within 45 days of the grant [119](#cite:119)
Check for current eligibility elsewhere before requesting a new investigation [119](#cite:119) [122](#cite:122)

name: Entity eligibility (facility clearance) and its sponsorship (32 CFR 117.9)
what: A firm cannot apply for its own [entity eligibility determination](#term:facility-clearance); a government contracting activity or a [cleared](#term:security-clearance) contractor [sponsors](#term:clearance-sponsorship) it when the firm needs access to compete or perform, on a legitimate government requirement [120](#cite:120) [146](#cite:146). The firm must be organised under U.S. law with a record of integrity; its senior management official, facility security officer and insider-threat official must hold eligibility; foreign ownership, control or influence must not be disqualifying [120](#cite:120). An [interim](#term:temporary-eligibility) determination is at the agency's sole discretion; while a determination is invalidated the firm may not bid on new classified work [120](#cite:120). [DCSA](#term:dcsa)'s roadmap puts the package review at day 20 and the key officials' [questionnaires](#term:sf-86) and fingerprints at day 45; the government funds the processing; no [end-to-end](#term:end-to-end-timeliness) time is given [146](#cite:146).
governing_text: 32 CFR §117.9; DCSA Facility Clearance Branch sponsorship roadmap
applies_when: Any firm without an entity eligibility determination that needs to hire or assign cleared staff [120](#cite:120)
steps: Find a sponsor with a bona fide need and the DD 254 or pre-award authorization [146](#cite:146)
Submit the NISS package; clear the SMO, FSO and ITPSO [120](#cite:120) [146](#cite:146)
Mitigate FOCI where it applies [120](#cite:120)

name: Temporary (interim) eligibility (SEAD 8; 32 CFR 117.10(l))
what: Government-wide policy on [temporary eligibility](#term:temporary-eligibility) dates from Security Executive Agent Directive 8 of May 18, 2020 [121](#cite:121); for contractors it is implemented at §117.10(l): granted only where no adverse information is found, limited to one year without approval, valid at its level but not for RD, COMSEC or NATO information before the final grant, with [SCI](#term:sensitive-compartmented-information) and SAP access a separate decision of the granting authority; non-U.S. citizens are ineligible; withdrawal is not a denial and cannot be appealed [119](#cite:119). No public figure reports how often contractor applicants receive it or how long the decision takes [127](#cite:127).
applies_when: A sponsored hire whose final determination will not arrive before the work must start [119](#cite:119)
steps: Submit the [questionnaire](#term:sf-86) and fingerprints; the determination follows the initial checks [119](#cite:119) [146](#cite:146)
Confirm the customer accepts an interim for the work and the facility ([synthesis](#term:synthesis-marker))

name: Reciprocity of investigations and adjudications (SEAD 7)
what: An agency accepts a background investigation and a national security adjudication by an authorized agency unless an exception applies: new adjudicatively relevant information; an investigation more than seven years old; an adjudication recorded with an exception; a [Bond Amendment disqualifier](#term:bond-amendment) where [SCI](#term:sensitive-compartmented-information), SAP or RD access is needed; an agency-specific requirement the Security Executive Agent approved; an [interim](#term:temporary-eligibility), limited or one-time grant; or a current denial or revocation, with ineligibility for at least a year [122](#cite:122). [Polygraphs](#term:polygraph) are accepted when they match the receiving agency's requirement, [reciprocity](#term:reciprocity) cannot be denied for want of one, and the polygraph is scheduled after a preliminary determination [122](#cite:122). The determination is due within five business days of receipt and records within ten [122](#cite:122). GAO found the government's reciprocity data inconsistent and incomplete, agency systems often lacking the needed information, and contractors left without status updates [145](#cite:145).
governing_text: SEAD 7 (effective November 9, 2018); 32 CFR §117.10(a)(6), (h)
applies_when: Any hire who holds or held eligibility granted by another agency or contractor sponsor [122](#cite:122)
steps: Collect level, investigation date and whether the grant was final [122](#cite:122)
Submit the request on acceptance; escalate at five business days [122](#cite:122) [145](#cite:145)

name: National security adjudicative guidelines (SEAD 4) and the Bond Amendment
what: Thirteen guidelines govern every eligibility decision: allegiance, foreign influence, foreign preference, sexual behaviour, personal conduct, financial considerations, alcohol, drug involvement, psychological conditions, criminal conduct, handling protected information, outside activities and use of information technology, weighed under the [whole-person concept](#term:adjudicative-guidelines), with listed conditions that raise and that mitigate each concern [123](#cite:123). The [Bond Amendment](#term:bond-amendment) bars eligibility outright for an unlawful drug user or addict, with no waiver, and bars [SCI](#term:sensitive-compartmented-information), SAP and RD access after a sentence with a year's incarceration, a dishonourable discharge or a finding of mental incompetence [123](#cite:123). The guidelines apply to contractors as covered individuals [123](#cite:123). A vendor's count of 624 published DOHA appeal decisions for 2024 found financial issues outnumbered all other issues combined [151](#cite:151).
governing_text: SEAD 4 (effective June 8, 2017), Appendices A and B; 50 U.S.C. 3343 (Bond Amendment)
applies_when: Every sponsored hire and every reciprocity exception for new information [123](#cite:123) [122](#cite:122)
steps: Do not pre-screen on the guidelines; the firm is not the adjudicator ([synthesis](#term:synthesis-marker))
Expect financial questions to be the common sticking point and the whole-person weighing to decide them [123](#cite:123) [151](#cite:151)
conflicts: The DOHA pattern rests on a vendor tally; the DOHA record itself is a todo [151](#cite:151).

name: E-Verify for federal contractors (FAR 22.18; 52.222-54)
what: The clause goes into solicitations and contracts over \$150,000 except work performed only outside the United States, periods of performance under 120 days, and commercial and COTS items [129](#cite:129). A contractor not yet enrolled enrolls as a federal contractor within 30 calendar days of award; new hires are verified within 3 business days after the date of hire; employees assigned to the contract within 90 calendar days of enrollment or award or 30 days after assignment, whichever is later [128](#cite:128). No re-verification is required for an employee already verified, holding an active Confidential, [Secret](#term:secret) or [Top Secret clearance](#term:top-secret), or credentialed after a completed HSPD-12 investigation [128](#cite:128). The clause flows down to service and construction [subcontracts](#term:subcontractor) over \$3,500 performed in the United States [128](#cite:128).
applies_when: Contracts over \$150,000, 120 days or longer, with work in the United States [129](#cite:129)
steps: Enroll within 30 days of award [128](#cite:128)
Initiate verification within 3 business days of each hire date [128](#cite:128)

name: Form I-9 employment eligibility verification (USCIS M-274)
what: Section 2 must be completed within three business days of the date employment begins, on the first day for a job of fewer than three business days [130](#cite:130). The employee chooses which acceptable documents to present and the employer cannot specify them; the documents are examined in the employee's physical presence unless the employer qualifies for the alternative procedure open to [E-Verify](#term:e-verify) participants; receipts are accepted for a limited period [130](#cite:130).
governing_text: 8 U.S.C. 1324a; USCIS Handbook for Employers M-274
applies_when: Every hire for pay in the United States [130](#cite:130)
steps: Section 1 by the first day; Section 2 within three business days [130](#cite:130)
Let the employee choose the documents; keep the export assessment on a separate form [130](#cite:130) [131](#cite:131)

name: Deemed exports and the U.S.-person rule in hiring (ITAR; DOJ employer fact sheet)
what: Releasing or transferring technical data to a foreign person in the United States is an export, deemed to go to every country of that person's citizenship or permanent residency [132](#cite:132). A [U.S. person](#term:us-person) is a lawful permanent resident or a protected individual under 8 U.S.C. 1324b(a)(3), which includes citizens, nationals, refugees and asylees [133](#cite:133) [131](#cite:131). The Justice Department's fact sheet tells employers not to state that the export rules require a citizenship, to assess only positions that work with controlled items, to keep that assessment apart from the [Form I-9](#term:form-i-9) without limiting document choice, and to apply to State or Commerce for an authorization before a non-U.S. person does the work [131](#cite:131). Settlements for "citizens only" postings ran from \$365,000 to \$500,000 per employer in 2023 [49](#cite:49) [50](#cite:50).
governing_text: 22 CFR §§120.50, 120.62; 15 CFR part 734 (EAR); 8 U.S.C. 1324b; DOJ IER employer fact sheet (rev. March 2024)
applies_when: Any position that handles ITAR or EAR technical data or items [131](#cite:131) [132](#cite:132)
steps: Identify the controlled positions and assess only those, after the offer and apart from the I-9 [131](#cite:131)
Apply for the authorization before a non-U.S. person is given access [131](#cite:131) [132](#cite:132)

Circuit [143](#cite:143) [225](#cite:225) [226](#cite:226).

name: Background reports under the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FTC employer guidance)
what: Before obtaining a [consumer report](#term:consumer-report) the employer gives a written, stand-alone disclosure that is not part of the application, obtains written permission, and certifies compliance to the reporting company [136](#cite:136). Before taking an adverse action it gives the person a copy of the report and the [summary of rights](#term:adverse-action-notice) so the person can dispute it; after the action it sends a notice with the reporting company's name and contact, a statement that the company did not make the decision, and the rights to dispute and to a free report within 60 days [136](#cite:136). Investigative reports built on interviews carry extra notices, and some states restrict [credit reports](#term:credit-check-law) in hiring [136](#cite:136).
governing_text: 15 U.S.C. 1681 et seq.; FTC business guidance (2016, modified 2020)
applies_when: Any hire screened through a third-party background report [136](#cite:136)
steps: Stand-alone disclosure and written permission before the report [136](#cite:136)
Pre-adverse-action notice with the report and the rights summary; adverse-action notice after [136](#cite:136)

pending_changes.text: New York State limits employer credit checks, joining fourteen states, DC and Puerto Rico; several of these laws except positions requiring a [security clearance](#term:security-clearance) [218](#cite:218).

The state credit-check and fair-chance overlays are states.yaml records (sweep 8) resting on vendor and advocacy compilations [216](#cite:216) [217](#cite:217) [218](#cite:218), statutes pending (t-8001).

name: Common Access Card sponsorship and investigative standards (32 CFR parts 157 and 161)
what: A contractor employee is [sponsored](#term:clearance-sponsorship) for a [CAC](#term:common-access-card) by a DoD official, and only for both physical access to a DoD facility and network logon, or recurring physical access to multiple facilities for six months or more [138](#cite:138). No card is issued without the required background investigation: at minimum a favourable FBI fingerprint check and a NACI or equivalent submitted to the investigative provider [138](#cite:138); a card may be issued on an [interim](#term:temporary-eligibility) basis on a favourable National Agency Check, with the final determination on the completed investigation [137](#cite:137). Interim credentials are not transferable or [reciprocally](#term:reciprocity) accepted; a denial or revocation can be reapplied for after one year; contractors are registered and re-verified every six months through TASS [137](#cite:137) [138](#cite:138). An employee credentialed after a completed HSPD-12 investigation is exempt from [E-Verify](#term:e-verify) re-verification [128](#cite:128).
governing_text: 32 CFR part 157 (79 FR 55624); 32 CFR §161.7 (79 FR 709, as amended); HSPD-12
applies_when: Any contractor hire who needs a DoD facility or network on a recurring basis [138](#cite:138)
steps: Government sponsor registers the request in TASS; fingerprints and the investigation submission precede issuance [138](#cite:138)
Interim card on a favourable National Agency Check; final on the completed investigation [137](#cite:137)

name: Cyberspace workforce qualification (DoDM 8140.03)
what: Contractors must be fully qualified for the cyberspace work roles they fill, and contracted support personnel must meet the [foundational qualification](#term:dod-8140), by education, training or a listed certification, on commencement of the work [139](#cite:139). Government and military personnel have nine months for the foundational and twelve for the resident qualification; anyone unqualified without a waiver is removed from the role; waivers are limited to severe [constraints](#term:constraint-record) and six months; twenty hours a year of continuing development are required [139](#cite:139). The manual's implementation ran to three years from February 2023 for all workforce elements [139](#cite:139).
governing_text: DoDM 8140.03 (February 15, 2023); DoDD 8140.01; the contract's cyber workforce terms
applies_when: Any DoD contract position coded to a cyberspace work role [139](#cite:139)
steps: Read the contract for the work-role codes and the qualification required [139](#cite:139)
Verify the foundational certification before the start date [139](#cite:139)

name: Drug-free workplace (FAR 26.5; 52.226-7) after the DFARS testing clause was reserved
what: Contracts above the simplified acquisition threshold, other than commercial products and services and work outside the United States, require a policy statement, an awareness program, employee reporting of workplace drug convictions within five days, notice to the contracting officer within ten and action within thirty; the subpart requires no [drug testing](#term:drug-free-workplace) [135](#cite:135). The DFARS clause that required DoD contractors on classified and other sensitive work to run a testing program, 252.223-7004, is reserved as of the May 7, 2026 DFARS change, and Part 223 no longer carries the drug-free work force subpart [134](#cite:134). Testing is therefore a matter of firm policy and state law, not a federal contract requirement, unless a customer writes one into the contract ([synthesis](#term:synthesis-marker)).
governing_text: 41 U.S.C. chapter 81; FAR subpart 26.5; FAR 52.226-7; DFARS 252.223-7004 (reserved)
applies_when: Contracts above the simplified acquisition threshold performed in the United States [135](#cite:135)
steps: Publish the policy and run the awareness program within 30 days of award [135](#cite:135)
Review any testing policy written for the old DFARS clause against state law (synthesis)

pending_changes.text: DFARS 252.223-7004 Drug-Free Work Force reserved; the rulemaking citation is a todo [134](#cite:134).

conflicts: The Federal Register notice that removed the DFARS clause was not found; the acquisition.gov page is the only source [134](#cite:134).

name: Title VII national security exception (42 U.S.C. 2000e-2(g))
what: It is not an unlawful employment practice to refuse to hire or to discharge an individual for a position subject to a requirement imposed in the interest of national security under a statute or executive order where the individual has not fulfilled or has ceased to fulfill that requirement [140](#cite:140). The exception covers the [clearance](#term:security-clearance) condition on an offer; it does not cover a citizenship restriction the law does not require, which remains a citizenship-status violation [131](#cite:131) [49](#cite:49).
applies_when: Any position conditioned on a clearance or another national-security requirement [140](#cite:140)
steps: Condition the offer on the requirement the contract imposes, not on a proxy for it [140](#cite:140) [131](#cite:131)

name: Training repayment and stay-or-pay provisions (CFPB; state laws; the withdrawn federal positions)
what: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau treats [training repayment provisions](#term:training-repayment-agreement) as employer-driven debt, found nearly 10 percent of workers covered in 2020, documented repayment demands far above training cost and usurious interest, and said it would evaluate them under consumer financial law [166](#cite:166). California bars, for contracts entered after January 1, 2026, any employment-contract term requiring repayment of training, education, relocation, signing or retention amounts for leaving before a date, with exceptions for a transferable credential under a separate, at-cost, prorated agreement, for [signing bonuses](#term:signing-bonus) on stated conditions, and for approved [apprenticeships](#term:registered-apprenticeship), and with no repayment on a termination except for misconduct; \$5,000 or actual damages, injunction and fees [167](#cite:167). Colorado allows repayment only for training distinct from normal on-the-job training, at reasonable cost declining proportionally over two years, with \$5,000 per worker penalties and consumer-credit treatment [168](#cite:168); Connecticut bars [promissory notes](#term:employment-promissory-note) as a condition of employment [168](#cite:168). The NLRB general counsel's memoranda against [stay-or-pay terms](#term:stay-or-pay-provision) were rescinded and the FTC rule that would have treated some provisions as [noncompetes](#term:noncompete-agreement) never took effect [168](#cite:168) [169](#cite:169).
governing_text: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16608 and Labor Code §926 (AB 692); Colo. Rev. Stat. §8-2-113; Conn. law; CFPB issue spotlight (2023)
applies_when: Any agreement that makes a worker repay training, a bonus or relocation on leaving; strictest where the worker is in California or Colorado [167](#cite:167) [168](#cite:168)
steps: Check the worker's state; the statutes go to states.yaml in sweep 8 [167](#cite:167) [168](#cite:168)
If a term is used at all: separate agreement, transferable credential, actual cost, prorated, no interest, nothing on termination without misconduct [167](#cite:167) [168](#cite:168)

pending_changes.text: California AB 692 applies to contracts entered after this date [167](#cite:167).

New York's Trapped at Work Act (signed 2025-12-19; chapter amendment 2026-02-13) makes employment promissory notes unenforceable, with exceptions for bonuses, relocation assistance and tuition for a transferable credential; fines \$1,000–\$5,000 per violation [212](#cite:212) [211](#cite:211).
Washington ESHB 1155 treats repayment and forfeiture terms tied to working in one's field as void noncompetes, excepting educational-expense agreements that expire within 18 months [210](#cite:210).

conflicts: The California, New York, Connecticut, Colorado and Wyoming terms rest on law-firm summaries [167](#cite:167) [168](#cite:168) [211](#cite:211) [212](#cite:212); Washington's is the statute [210](#cite:210); states.yaml carries the per-state overlay (sweep 8) with the statutes pending (t-8001).

name: Noncompete agreements after the FTC rule's vacatur
what: The 2024 federal rule banning most [noncompetes](#term:noncompete-agreement) was held beyond the Commission's authority by a district court; on September 5, 2025 the Commission voted 3–1 to dismiss its appeals and accede to the vacatur, leaving noncompetes to state law and to case-by-case enforcement [169](#cite:169). The state map (bans, income thresholds, notice rules) is a sweep-8 record. A noncompete on a trained and [cleared](#term:security-clearance) engineer is therefore a state question and a retention question, not a federal one ([synthesis](#term:synthesis-marker)).
governing_text: Ryan LLC v. FTC (N.D. Tex. 2024), vacatur acceded to September 5, 2025; state statutes
applies_when: Any restrictive covenant in an offer or a training agreement [169](#cite:169)
steps: Check the state before drafting; the federal rule is gone [169](#cite:169)

pending_changes.text: Tennessee HB 1034 voids noncompetes for workers earning under \$70,000 [209](#cite:209).

Washington ESHB 1155 voids every noncompetition covenant regardless of signing date, keeps [nonsolicitation terms](#term:non-solicitation-agreement) capped at 18 months and requires notice to affected workers by 2027-10-01 [210](#cite:210).

name: Compensable training time under the FLSA (29 CFR 785.27)
what: For non-exempt employees, time in lectures, meetings and training programs counts as hours worked unless all four conditions hold: outside normal hours, voluntary, not job related, and no other work performed at the same time [170](#cite:170). Required [onboarding](#term:onboarding), certification study the job needs and in-hours courses are paid time ([synthesis](#term:synthesis-marker) from [170](#cite:170)).
governing_text: 29 U.S.C. 201 et seq.; 29 CFR 785.27–785.32; DOL Fact Sheet #22
applies_when: Any training of non-exempt staff; exempt professionals are outside the rule but the cost rules still apply [170](#cite:170) [175](#cite:175)
steps: Treat required and job-related training as paid hours unless all four conditions are met [170](#cite:170)

name: Allowability of training and education costs (FAR 31.205-44)
what: Training and education related to the field in which the employee works or may reasonably be expected to work are [allowable costs](#term:allowable-cost), except overtime for training, salaries for attending undergraduate or part-time graduate classes in working hours absent unusual circumstances, full-time graduate education beyond two school years or the program length, grants and scholarships to institutions, training for other than bona fide employees, and contributions to dependents' college savings [175](#cite:175). The allowable cost sits in the indirect pools and the rates [148](#cite:148).
applies_when: Cost-type contracts and any contract whose rates are built from allowable cost [175](#cite:175)
steps: Keep training to employees and to the field of the work; document the relation [175](#cite:175)
Budget it in the [indirect rates](#term:overhead-rate) for the cost accounting period [148](#cite:148)

name: Educational assistance programs (IRC §127)
what: Up to \$5,250 per employee per calendar year of [educational assistance](#term:section-127-plan) is excludable from wages, the amount adjusted for the cost of living for taxable years after 2026; it covers tuition, fees, books, supplies and equipment, and since March 27, 2020, with no end date after the 2025 amendments, principal and interest on the employee's own qualified education loans; the program must be a separate written plan for the exclusive benefit of employees, and employees must be told it exists and what its terms are [174](#cite:174).
governing_text: 26 U.S.C. §127; IRS FS-2026-10; Publication 5993 (sample plan)
applies_when: Any employer paying for an employee's education or student loans [174](#cite:174)
steps: Adopt the written plan; notify employees; track the \$5,250 per person per year [174](#cite:174)

pending_changes.text: The \$5,250 limit is indexed for taxable years beginning after 2026 [174](#cite:174).

name: Reporting duties and continuous vetting for cleared employees (32 CFR 117.8; SEAD 3)
what: The contractor reports to the cognizant security agency adverse information about [cleared](#term:security-clearance) employees from verified sources, and the duty survives the employee's termination; suspicious contacts; deaths, name changes, terminations and citizenship changes; an employee who no longer wants eligibility or classified work; refusal to sign the SF 312; and changes in the firm's ownership, name, address, key management personnel, bankruptcy or foreign ownership [189](#cite:189). Cleared employees themselves report under SEAD 3: unofficial foreign travel at least five days before departure, continuing foreign contacts, foreign financial interests, bankruptcies, liens, garnishments and debts over 120 days delinquent, arrests, alcohol or drug treatment, cohabitants and marriages, conflicting outside employment, and concerns about other cleared individuals; failure to report can affect eligibility [190](#cite:190). Enrolment in [continuous vetting](#term:continuous-vetting) covered 78 percent of the population in FY2026 Q3, industry about 984,000 enrollments [54](#cite:54) [126](#cite:126).
governing_text: 32 CFR §117.8; SEAD 3 (2016); SEAD 6 (continuous evaluation); Trusted Workforce 2.0
applies_when: Every contractor with cleared employees, throughout employment and at separation [189](#cite:189)
steps: Brief each cleared hire on the SEAD 3 self-reporting list and the firm's reporting channel [190](#cite:190)
Report terminations and status changes; keep reporting adverse information after separation [189](#cite:189)

pending_changes.text: Full continuous-vetting enrolment planned for September 2028 [54](#cite:54).

name: Key-personnel substitution and notice clauses (agency clauses; HHSAR 352.237-75 as the example)
what: Where a contract names [key personnel](#term:key-personnel-clause), they are essential to performance and cannot be diverted, replaced or announced as changed without the contracting officer's written consent; the HHS clause requires at least 30 days' notice before a voluntary move with a justification and a replacement whose skills, experience and credentials meet or exceed the requirement, and the maximum practicable notice when a person is terminated for cause or leaves on less than 30 days [188](#cite:188). Before award, a proposed key person's unavailability must be reported at GAO's standard [108](#cite:108). Other agencies' clauses set their own periods and standards (todo).
governing_text: Agency key-personnel clauses (e.g., 48 CFR 352.237-75); the solicitation's key-personnel terms; GAO Orion
applies_when: Any contract or proposal naming key personnel [188](#cite:188) [108](#cite:108)
steps: Read the clause for the notice period and the approval standard before any move [188](#cite:188)
Keep a qualified substitute identified for each named person [188](#cite:188)
